passage: After losing the final round for the fifth time in a row, Omar slumped in his chair in the Nairobi flat, jaw tight. A chat message popped up from a teammate called Ivan: "That was rough. You okay? 🙂" Omar blinked. Nobody usually asked. A warm feeling spread through his chest, and for a second he wanted to tell Ivan everything, even his school's name. His fingers paused over the keys. He typed, "Just annoyed. Thanks." Ivan wrote, "Happens to me too. Good game." Omar kept the chat to the game, and when he switched off he told Dad about the friendly teammate.

qa.q: What did Ivan write to Omar after the lost round?
qa.a: Ivan wrote, "That was rough. You okay?"

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Ivan's message appeared, and what made him pause?
qa.a: He felt surprised and warmed because nobody usually asked, and he had a moment of wanting to share everything; then his fingers paused, showing he remembered to be careful.

qa.q: How can Omar stay friendly and safe with an online teammate?
qa.a: Reply kindly, keep the chat about the game, never share private things like his school, and tell Dad about it, as he did.

qa.q: How might Ivan see the moment?
qa.a: As a friendly teammate noticing that someone looked upset after losing; Ivan's message and "Happens to me too" read as simple kindness, though Omar still cannot know Ivan well.

grounding: Illustrates a child touched by a stranger's kindness after losing a game who stays friendly but shares no private information.

passage: Tuesday. A message came in the games chat today from a person called Vinita: "Hi! Your drawing in the gallery is so cool. Want to talk?" I wanted to reply so much. My fingers were already on the keys. Nobody has ever said my drawing was cool except Ammi. But I remembered the rule, so I showed Ammi first. She read it and said we would look at the profile together and she would decide about replying. I felt impatient, then relieved. I did not tell this person anything about where I live or my school. - Rafiq

qa.q: What did the message from Vinita say about Rafiq's drawing?
qa.a: It said Rafiq's drawing in the gallery is so cool.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling while holding back from replying?
qa.a: Eager and curious to reply, then impatient, and finally relieved after showing Ammi.

qa.q: Why is it wise for Rafiq to check with Ammi before chatting?
qa.a: A parent can look at the profile with Rafiq and spot warning signs a child might miss, and Rafiq keeps school, address and photos private.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the message?
qa.a: With care for Rafiq's safety rather than anger: she read it, wanted to look at the profile together and said she would decide about replying.

grounding: Illustrates a child curious about a message from an online stranger who checks with a parent first and shares no private details.

passage: Monday. A stranger messaged Tenzin in a game chat. "You are so mature for your age. Not like the other kids." Tenzin felt his cheeks warm and sat a little taller. Wednesday. The stranger wrote again. "Our chats are special. Don't tell anyone, not even your parents." Tenzin's stomach went tight. He remembered a school talk about secrets that make you uneasy. Friday. He stopped replying and told Binita Ma'am, his class teacher, at the end of the day. She stayed with him and said, "This is not your fault. You have done nothing wrong. Thank you for telling me." She told the school safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that evening.

qa.q: On which day did Tenzin tell Binita Ma'am?
qa.a: He told her on Friday.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel on Monday, and what changed by Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he felt flattered, his cheeks warm and sitting taller; by Wednesday the request to keep it secret made his stomach go tight and uneasy.

qa.q: What should a child do when a stranger flatters them and asks for secrecy?
qa.a: Stop replying and tell a parent or teacher, as Tenzin did with Binita Ma'am 🤍.

qa.q: How might Binita Ma'am see Tenzin's decision to tell her?
qa.a: As a brave and sensible step: she stayed with him, said it was not his fault, told the safeguarding lead and helped him tell his parents that same evening.

grounding: Illustrates a child flattered by an online stranger who asks for secrecy, recognising the warning and telling a teacher.

passage: Mridul was in the back room of the village shop, using the shop phone, when a message from a stranger came. "I know where you live. I know your house near the banyan tree." His hands went cold. His mouth would not work. He did not answer. He did not delete it either. His older brother Sumit came in and saw his face. Mridul held out the phone. Sumit read it and his jaw tightened, but his voice stayed steady. "Come. We tell Papa now." Papa listened, thanked Mridul for showing him, and said there were people whose job it is to help with this.

qa.q: What did Mridul do with the stranger's message?
qa.a: He did not answer it and did not delete it.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when the message came, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was scared and frozen: his hands went cold and his mouth would not work.

qa.q: What steps should a child take after such a message?
qa.a: Do not reply, keep the messages, and tell a trusted adult straight away, as Mridul did with Sumit and Papa.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt reading the message?
qa.a: Worried and angry, since his jaw tightened, but steady enough to take Mridul to Papa at once 🤍.

grounding: Illustrates a child frozen by a stranger's message claiming to know where he lives who keeps it, does not reply and tells a trusted adult.

passage: Yash sat on the bench outside the counsellor's room, thumbs pressed together. The corridor smelled of floor cleaner and somewhere a class was chanting tables. He had asked to see Aadhya Ma'am. When she opened the door he stood up too fast. "I was messaging a person I should have ignored," he said. "I told them things. My parents will be so angry." His eyes stayed on the floor. Aadhya Ma'am said, "Come in. Take your time." She did not say anything about how it was his fault. She offered to sit with him while he called his mother, and asked if he wanted that.

qa.q: Where did Yash wait before seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: He waited on the bench outside the counsellor's room.

qa.q: What is Yash afraid of about telling his parents, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He fears they will be very angry and maybe feels ashamed; he kept his eyes on the floor and rushed to say his parents would be so angry.

qa.q: What is the safest step for Yash now?
qa.a: Tell his parents early, with Aadhya Ma'am there to support him, rather than keeping it secret.

qa.q: How might Yash's parents feel when they hear?
qa.a: Probably worried first, but on his side, and glad that he told them early.

grounding: Illustrates a child ashamed of an online chat with someone he should not have chatted with who finds the courage to tell adults.

passage: Yash, sit down. I'm your Mausi Aadhya, and this happened when I was eleven. My friend Ritika showed me her phone. Someone she had never met was asking her for pictures of herself. She begged me, "Promise you won't tell." I promised, and then I lay awake all night. I was afraid she would hate me. But I was more afraid for her. In the morning I told my mother everything. She listened, told me I had done nothing wrong, and phoned Ritika's mother that same evening. Ritika was furious with me for a week. She wouldn't sit next to me. Later, she came and said, "Thank you." I still remember how heavy that night felt.

qa.q: How old was Aadhya when this happened?
qa.a: She was eleven.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling on the night before she told her mother?
qa.a: She was torn: she was afraid Ritika would hate her, but more afraid for Ritika's safety, and she lay awake all night.

qa.q: What would you advise a child whose friend shows such a chat?
qa.a: Tell a trusted adult even if the friend gets angry, because the friend's safety matters more than the promise.

qa.q: How might Ritika have felt at first, and how did that change?
qa.a: She was furious for a week, probably feeling betrayed, and then came and thanked Aadhya once she saw it kept her safe.

grounding: Illustrates a child breaking a friend's secret about a stranger asking for photos, telling an adult out of loyalty to the friend's safety.

passage: On Thursday evening Vandana opened the class group chat on Mummy's phone. Madhuri had written a mean line about her dress and other kids had added laughing faces. Vandana's cheeks burned and her thumbs shook. She typed an angry reply and then deleted it. She took a screenshot instead. It felt as though the whole class was staring at her. She went to the kitchen behind the family's kirana shop and showed Mummy, who read it twice. "This is not your fault," Mummy said. Next morning they showed the class teacher, who said they would talk to Madhuri and the class about the chat.

qa.q: What did Vandana do instead of sending her angry reply?
qa.a: She deleted it and took a screenshot instead.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling as she read the message in the group chat?
qa.a: Hurt and exposed, as if the whole class were staring, and angry enough to type a reply before deleting it.

qa.q: What steps helped Vandana handle the message?
qa.a: She saved the proof, did not reply in anger and told Mummy and then the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have seen the message she wrote?
qa.a: Perhaps as a joke to get laughs from others, without thinking how much it would hurt, though the passage does not say what Madhuri was thinking.

grounding: Illustrates a child hurt by a classmate's mean group-chat message who saves proof, does not reply in anger and tells adults.

passage: In the Pune flat, Gurleen curled up on the sofa with Papa's tablet and typed question after question to the AI assistant. Why do volcanoes erupt? How many legs does a spider have? The answers appeared in seconds, and she squealed each time. Her older brother Nilesh looked up from his homework. "Don't just believe it, Gurleen. Check it in the encyclopedia." Later she found one answer that didn't match her science book. She frowned, then carried both to school and asked her teacher, who showed her which to trust. Gurleen still loved asking, but she liked knowing where to check.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask the AI assistant about?
qa.a: She asked why volcanoes erupt and how many legs a spider has.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as the answers appeared, and what made her check one?
qa.a: She was delighted and curious, squealing at each answer; she checked one because it did not match her science book.

qa.q: How can Gurleen use the AI assistant for learning?
qa.a: Keep asking, then double-check with books and teachers, as she did with her science book and her teacher 🙂.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Gurleen's questions?
qa.a: With approval for her curiosity, while nudging her to check facts in the encyclopedia rather than simply believing the assistant.

grounding: Illustrates a child curious and delighted by an AI assistant who double-checks with books and a teacher.

passage: Reena typed her whole maths worksheet into the AI assistant and copied the answers into her notebook. She sat back, relieved, with an hour to spare. The next day the teacher called her to the board to solve the first sum. Her mind was blank. Yusuf whispered, "Isn't that from yesterday's homework?" Her ears burned. That evening she asked the assistant to explain how to do the sums step by step, and then covered the screen and tried the next ones on her own. She got two wrong, checked the steps again and got the third right.

qa.q: Who whispered to Reena at the board?
qa.a: Yusuf whispered to her.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling at the board, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt panic and embarrassment: her mind went blank and her ears burned.

qa.q: What is a better way for Reena to use the AI assistant for homework?
qa.a: Ask it to explain the steps, then close it and try the sums herself, as she did that evening 😊.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have seen Reena's blank moment at the board?
qa.a: Yusuf was probably puzzled, since the sum came from yesterday's homework, and the whisper looks like an attempt to help her remember.

grounding: Illustrates a child relying on an AI to do homework, unable to answer in class, and then using it to explain before trying herself.

passage: In the school computer lab, Devika typed her river project into the AI assistant. It said, in a calm, sure voice, exactly how long the river was and where it began. She copied it down without a second thought. Manjula Ma'am stopped by her desk. "How do you know that's right?" Devika blinked. "The computer said it. It sounded so sure." Manjula Ma'am opened the atlas beside her. The length in the atlas was different. Devika's face went pink. "So it can be wrong even when it sounds sure?" "Yes," said Manjula Ma'am, "so what will you do for facts that matter?"

qa.q: Where was Devika when she typed her river project into the assistant?
qa.a: She was in the school computer lab.

qa.q: Why did Devika believe the assistant so completely?
qa.a: Because it sounded calm and sure, and she took that confidence to mean it was right.

qa.q: What could Devika do for important facts in her project?
qa.a: Check them in a second source such as the atlas or with her teacher, especially when the answer sounds sure.

qa.q: How might Manjula Ma'am see the moment at Devika's desk?
qa.a: As a chance for Devika to learn to check rather than to be scolded: she asked how Devika knew and opened the atlas beside her.

grounding: Illustrates a child believing an AI's confident answer until an atlas shows a mistake, learning to check important facts.
